n: Joel looks to the future “in those days,” when the Lord gathers back His scattered people of Judah and Jerusalem. This connects to the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.g: Restore the fortunes of; bring back the exiles.

n: The Lord will gather the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them for scattering Israel and dividing His land.

f.g: The name means “Jehovah judges.” Tradition places it in the Kidron Valley next to Jerusalem.
Enter into judgment with them, as in a court case.

n: The nations treated God’s people as cheap goods, gambling for them and trading children for a prostitute or a drink. God sees every injustice done to the vulnerable.
The Lord addresses the coastal cities. Do they think they can pay Him back for something? Whatever harm they intend will quickly fall on their own heads.

f.g: Phoenician trading cities on the coast north of Israel, in modern Lebanon.
Philistia — the land of the Philistines on the southwest coast.

n: They looted the Lord’s silver and gold and the treasures of His temple and put them in their own temples.
Worse, they sold people of Judah as slaves to the Greeks, far from their homeland. Slave trading through Phoenician ports was well known in the ancient world.

f.g: Hebrew Yevanim — Ionians, Greeks living around the Aegean Sea.

n: God promises to bring the enslaved back from wherever they were sold, and to repay their captors.
Justice will be reversed: the slave traders’ own children will be sold, and sent to the Sabeans in distant Arabia.

f.g: People of Sheba in southern Arabia, famous long-distance traders.

n: Now the Lord issues a challenge to the nations: Prepare for war! Gather your strongest soldiers! This is an ironic summons to a battle they cannot win.

f.g: Literally “sanctify war” — ancient armies performed rituals before battle.

n: Joel turns a famous peace promise upside down: turn farm tools into weapons. Even weaklings should claim to be strong. (Isaiah and Micah foresee the opposite in the Messiah’s reign.)
The nations are told to assemble, and Joel prays for the Lord to bring down His own mighty ones — His heavenly armies.

f.g: The Lord’s warriors — likely His angelic hosts.

n: The nations come to the valley of Jehoshaphat, and the Lord sits as Judge. The battlefield becomes a courtroom.

f.w: there will I sit to judge

n: Harvest images describe judgment: swing the sickle, for the crop is ripe; tread the grapes, for the winepress overflows — their wickedness is full.

f.w: Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

n: Huge crowds fill “the valley of decision” — the place where the Lord delivers His verdict. The day of the Lord is near.

f.g: The Hebrew suggests a verdict or sharp cutting — God’s decision, not man’s.

n: Sun, moon, and stars go dark — the same cosmic signs from chapter 2, showing this is the great day of the Lord.

f.w: The sun and the moon shall be darkened

n: The Lord roars like a lion from Zion and shakes heaven and earth. Yet for His own people He is a refuge and strength.
Then everyone will know that the Lord lives in Zion. Jerusalem will be holy, and no foreign invader will pass through it again.
A picture of paradise: mountains drip with wine, hills flow with milk, and a fountain springs from the temple to water the dry valley. Ezekiel saw a similar river from the temple.

f.w: a fountain shall come forth of the house of the LORD

f.g: “Valley of acacias” — a dry valley, perhaps toward the Dead Sea.

n: Egypt and Edom, longtime enemies who shed innocent blood in Judah, will become wastelands.
In contrast, Judah and Jerusalem will be inhabited forever — a promise of lasting security for God’s people.
The book ends with cleansing and presence: the Lord will purify His people and dwell in Zion. God with His people is the final hope.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean God will avenge their blood or will declare them innocent; either way, He sets things right.
